p1.key: Mg reduces Zn2+, and Zn reduces Cu2+, so the reducing strength is Mg > Zn > Cu. Magnesium metal is the strongest reducing agent; ions such as Cu2+ act as oxidizing agents.
Pb2+ has the more positive E° so it is reduced, and Sn is oxidized. E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = −0.13 − (−0.14) = +0.01 V. A spontaneous cell has a positive e.m.f.
ΔG° = −nFE°. A and B both transfer 2 electrons, and B has the larger E° (0.62 V), so it gives the most negative ΔG°. C and D have negative E°, so ΔG° is positive.
Cl goes from −1 in Cl<sup>−</sup> to +1 in OCl<sup>−</sup>: oxidation, so an oxidizing agent is needed. In B, S stays +6. C (H<sup>+</sup> → H<sub>2</sub>) and D (S +2.5 → +2) are reductions.
Ag+ has the more positive E°, so it is reduced and Sn is oxidized: Sn + 2Ag+ → Sn2+ + 2Ag. E°cell = 0.80 − (−0.14) = +0.94 V. Do not double E° when you balance the electrons.
Charge = It = 0.2 × 3600 C. At the anode, 2H<sub>2</sub>O → O<sub>2</sub> + 4H<sup>+</sup> + 4e<sup>−</sup>, so mol O<sub>2</sub> = It/(4 × 96500). Mass = (0.2 × 60 × 60 × 32)/(4 × 96500).
p1.flag: Faraday's law calculations not in 2025 guide

p1.key: Na<sup>+</sup> is attracted to the negative electrode (cathode), where it gains an electron: Na<sup>+</sup> + e<sup>−</sup> → Na. Gaining electrons is reduction.

A reducing agent must be able to lose electrons. Fe<sup>2+</sup> can be oxidized to Fe<sup>3+</sup>. Ca<sup>2+</sup>, Cu<sup>2+</sup> and Zn<sup>2+</sup> are already in their usual highest oxidation states and cannot be oxidized further.
Cu2+ (E° = +0.339 V) is reduced and Tl (−0.336 V) is oxidized: 2Tl + Cu2+ → 2Tl+ + Cu. E°cell = 0.339 − (−0.336) = +0.675 V. E° values are not doubled.
Mg2+ + 2e− → Mg and 2Cl− → Cl2 + 2e−. The same 2 mol of electrons produces 1 mol Mg and 1 mol Cl2.
In N<sub>2</sub>O<sub>4</sub> → 2NO<sub>2</sub>, nitrogen is +4 on both sides, so no oxidation states change. A, C and D all involve changes (D is a disproportionation of O from −1 to −2 and 0).
2O2− → O2 + 4e−, so 0.2 mol O2 needs 0.8 mol electrons. Na+ + e− → Na, so the same charge gives 0.8 mol Na.
p1.flag: Faraday-type electrolysis quantities not in 2025 guide

p1.key: Zn and Co both displace Ag, so Ag is least reactive. Co does not displace Zn, so Zn is more reactive than Co: Ag < Co < Zn.
Butanone is a ketone. LiAlH4 reduces it to butan-2-ol, but acidified dichromate cannot oxidize ketones further (no H on the carbonyl carbon): I only.

Mn is +7 in MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> and O is −2. Acidified permanganate is a strong oxidizing agent (E° = +1.51 V) and can oxidize Br<sup>−</sup> (E° Br<sub>2</sub>/Br<sup>−</sup> = +1.09 V) but not F<sup>−</sup> (+2.87 V).

The statement that is not correct is A. In a molten salt the ions are free to move all the time; applying a voltage simply makes them drift towards the electrodes. B, C and D are correct descriptions of electrolysis.
Electrode potential depends on the half-cell reaction (the electrode material), the concentration and the temperature. The surface area of the electrode does not affect it.
The mass deposited depends on the charge passed (current × time) and on the number of electrons needed per ion (its charge). The voltage between the electrodes does not affect it.
p1.flag: Faraday's law not in 2025 guide

p1.key: In 2CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> → Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup>, Cr stays at +6 and O at −2, so nothing is oxidized or reduced (it is an acid–base reaction). C is a disproportionation of Mn(+6) to +7 and +4.

The Sn<sup>4+</sup>/Sn<sup>2+</sup> couple has the lower E° (0.15 V), so Sn<sup>2+</sup> is more easily oxidized and is the better reducing agent. E°<sub>cell</sub> = 0.77 − 0.15 = 0.62 V; E° values are never multiplied by stoichiometric coefficients.

In aqueous NaCl, water is reduced at the cathode: 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 2e⁻ → H<sub>2</sub> + 2OH⁻, so 2 mol e⁻ give 1 mol H<sub>2</sub>. The molten cell gives 2 mol Na, not 1, and Cl<sub>2</sub> forms at anodes, not cathodes.
2-methylpropan-1-ol is a primary alcohol: it oxidizes to an aldehyde (alkanal), then a carboxylic acid, and burns to CO2 and H2O. Only secondary alcohols give ketones (alkanones).
In CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> → Cr<sup>3+</sup>, chromium goes from +6 to +3: a decrease in oxidation state is reduction. A and D are oxidations of Mn; in C, Cr stays at +6.
E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = −1.18 − (−1.66) = +0.48 V. Al (more negative E°) is oxidized; E° values are not multiplied by coefficients.

At the negative electrode Cu<sup>2+</sup> is reduced to copper metal (more easily reduced than water). At the positive electrode, chlorine forms from concentrated chloride solutions but oxygen from dilute ones, so both C and D were accepted.
Propanal (an aldehyde) is oxidized by acidified dichromate to propanoic acid. Ketones (propanone), carboxylic acids and tertiary alcohols ((CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COH) are not oxidized.
Bromine starts at 0. In Br<sup>−</sup> it is −1 (reduced) and in BrO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> it is +5 (oxidized), so Br<sub>2</sub> undergoes disproportionation.

At the cathode (−), Pb<sup>2+</sup> gains electrons: Pb<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup> → Pb (reduction). At the anode (+), Br<sup>−</sup> loses electrons: 2Br<sup>−</sup> → Br<sub>2</sub> + 2e<sup>−</sup> (oxidation).

Z has the most positive E° (+1.36 V), so it is the strongest oxidizing agent and can oxidize both X<sup>−</sup> (+1.09 V) and Y<sup>−</sup> (+0.54 V). (These match Cl<sub>2</sub>, Br<sub>2</sub> and I<sub>2</sub>.)
One faraday = 1 mol e<sup>−</sup>. It deposits 1 mol Ag (108 g), ½ mol Ni (59/2 = 29.5 g) and ⅓ mol Cr (52/3 = 17.3 g).
p1.flag: Faraday calculations not in 2025 syllabus

p1.key: I is the reduction of the aldehyde propanal to propan-1-ol, using LiAlH<sub>4</sub> (or NaBH<sub>4</sub>). II is the oxidation of the aldehyde to propanoic acid, using acidified dichromate(VI).
The less reactive metal (Cu) has the ion that is most easily reduced, so Cu<sup>2+</sup> is the strongest oxidizing agent. Metal atoms (Mg, Cu) act as reducing agents.
p1.flag: duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: In C, Cr goes from +6 in K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> to +3 in Cr<sub>2</sub>(SO<sub>4</sub>)<sub>3</sub> (Cl<sup>−</sup> is oxidized to Cl<sub>2</sub>). Cr stays at +3 in A and B and at +6 in D.
p1.flag: duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: Half-equations: SO32− + H2O → SO42− + 2H+ + 2e− and Ce4+ + e− → Ce3+. Balancing electrons needs 2 Ce4+.
p1.flag: duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: Fe3+/Fe2+ (+0.77 V) is reduced and Fe/Fe2+ (−0.44 V) oxidized: Fe + 2Fe3+ → 3Fe2+. E°cell = 0.77 − (−0.44) = +1.21 V.
p1.flag: duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: The amount of tin depends on the charge passed (Q = It), so doubling either the current or the time doubles the tin. Sn4+ needs 4 e− per atom instead of 2, which would halve the amount.
p1.flag: quantitative electrolysis not in 2025 syllabus; duplicate of 2003M paper (identical images and markscheme)

p1.key: Cr goes from +3 in Cr<sup>3+</sup> to +6 in CrO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> (x − 8 = −2). An increase in oxidation state is oxidation.

The reactions show the reducing strength order Fe > Cd > Sn > Pb. A metal reduces the ions of any metal below it, so Cd + Pb<sup>2+</sup> and Fe + Pb<sup>2+</sup> react, but Sn cannot reduce Fe<sup>2+</sup>.
Pb → Pb2+ + 2e− (×3); NO3− + 4H+ + 3e− → NO + 2H2O (×2). Overall: 3Pb + 2NO3− + 8H+ → 3Pb2+ + 2NO + 4H2O.
ΔG° = −nFE°, so a positive E° gives a negative ΔG°, which means the reaction is spontaneous.

Amount of product depends on the charge passed (current × time) and on how many electrons each ion needs, i.e. its charge (e.g. Cu<sup>2+</sup> needs 2 mol e<sup>−</sup> per mol Cu, Ag<sup>+</sup> only 1).
p1.flag: quantitative (Faraday) electrolysis not in 2025 guide

p1.key: S is +4 in H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub> and +6 in HSO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>, so H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>3</sub> is oxidized and is the reducing agent. Sn<sup>4+</sup> is reduced to Sn<sup>2+</sup>, making it the oxidizing agent.
In a voltaic cell the positive electrode is the cathode (reduction). In an electrolytic cell the positive electrode is the anode, attracting anions, which are oxidized.
Cu<sup>2+</sup>/Cu has the most positive E°, so Cu<sup>2+</sup> is the strongest oxidizing agent here and oxidizes both Mg and Zn. Zn cannot reduce Mg<sup>2+</sup>, and Cu cannot reduce either ion.
Cd2+ is reduced (cathode) and Cr oxidized (anode): E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = −0.40 − (−0.75) = +0.35 V. Stoichiometric coefficients do not change E°.

At the positive electrode (anode) anions or water are oxidized. In very dilute NaCl, water is oxidized to O<sub>2</sub>; in concentrated NaCl, Cl<sup>−</sup> is oxidized to Cl<sub>2</sub>. Na and H<sub>2</sub> would form at the negative electrode.

Acidified dichromate(VI) oxidizes primary (II) and secondary (I) alcohols, turning from orange Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> to green Cr<sup>3+</sup>. Tertiary alcohols (III) are not oxidized.
H is +1 and O is −2. For neutral H2SO4: 2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0, so S = +6.

Zinc is oxidized (Zn → Zn<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup>), so it loses electrons that flow to the copper half-cell. Copper is deposited (its mass increases), and anions move through the salt bridge towards the zinc half-cell.

SO<sub>2</sub> + 2H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + 2H<sup>+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup>. S goes from +4 to +6 (oxidation), so electrons appear on the right, and 2H<sup>+</sup> balance H and charge on the right.

The SHE uses H<sub>2</sub> gas at 1 atm (now 100 kPa), 1.0 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> H<sup>+</sup> (not 1.0 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>, which gives 2 mol dm<sup>−3</sup> H<sup>+</sup>), 298 K and a platinum electrode.

The amount of product depends on the charge passed (current × time), and the Cl<sup>−</sup> concentration decides whether Cl<sub>2</sub> or O<sub>2</sub> forms at the anode. Temperature and pressure (A, B, D) are not the deciding factors.
Oxidizing a primary alcohol (butan-1-ol) gives the aldehyde butanal (distil it off). Butan-2-ol gives butanone; butanone and butanoic acid are not converted to butanal.
Mg goes from 0 to +2 (oxidized) and H from +1 to 0 (reduced). A, C and D are acid reactions with a base or carbonate where no oxidation states change.
Z displaces Y from its sulfate, so Z is more reactive than Y. X does not displace Y, so Y is more reactive than X: Z > Y > X.
MnO4− + 8H+ + 5e− → Mn2+ + 4H2O (Mn: +7 → +2). Coefficients: 1 + 8 + 5 + 1 + 4 = 19.

Fe<sup>3+</sup>/Fe<sup>2+</sup> (+0.77 V) is more positive than Ni<sup>2+</sup>/Ni (−0.23 V), so Fe<sup>3+</sup> is reduced while Ni is oxidized. Ca<sup>2+</sup> is far too weak an oxidizing agent to oxidize Ni.

Water is oxidized at the positive electrode, releasing colourless O<sub>2</sub>. Copper is deposited on the negative electrode (its mass increases) and the blue colour fades as Cu<sup>2+</sup> is removed.
Oxidizing a secondary alcohol with acidified dichromate(VI) gives a ketone in one step. Aldehydes and carboxylic acids come from primary alcohols.
Propanone is a ketone, which is not readily oxidized. Propan-1-ol, propan-2-ol and propanal are all oxidized by acidified dichromate(VI).

Mg is more reactive, so it is the anode and is oxidized, losing electrons, which flow to the iron half-cell where Fe<sup>2+</sup> is reduced (so [Fe<sup>2+</sup>] falls). Anions move towards the Mg half-cell.

The object is the negative electrode (cathode), where Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup> → Cu. The copper anode dissolves at the same rate, so the positive electrode loses mass and [Cu<sup>2+</sup>] stays constant.
E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode = +0.80 − (−0.13) = +0.93 V. Do not multiply the Ag value by 2: E° does not depend on stoichiometry.
The same charge passes through both cells. Sn2+ and Cu2+ both need 2 electrons per atom, so equal amounts are deposited: 0.01 mol Cu.
p1.flag: quantitative electrolysis not in 2025 guide

p1.key: In a molten salt the ions are mobile: cations move to the negative electrode and anions to the positive electrode. Electrons flow only in the external circuit, not through the electrolyte.

For copper plating: the spoon is the cathode, copper is the anode (it dissolves, replacing Cu²⁺), and the electrolyte contains Cu²⁺(aq). A copper cathode (III) is wrong because the spoon must be the cathode.
E°cell = E°(reduction) − E°(oxidation) = +0.52 − (+0.15) = +0.37 V. The half-cell with the more positive E° (Cu⁺/Cu) is reduced; Cu⁺ is oxidized to Cu²⁺ in the other half-cell.
ΔG° = −nFE°<sub>cell</sub>, so a spontaneous cell reaction has positive E°<sub>cell</sub> and negative ΔG°.

The amount of copper deposited depends on the charge passed (current × time). Increasing the time by 10 % increases the charge, and so the copper mass, by 10 %. Concentration, electrode area and temperature do not directly change the charge passed at a given current.
Balanced: 8H⁺ + MnO4⁻ + 5e⁻ → Mn²⁺ + 4H2O. Total coefficients = 8 + 1 + 5 + 1 + 4 = 19.
A primary alcohol can be oxidized directly to an aldehyde, or dehydrated to an alkene (e.g. with hot conc. acid). Ketones come from oxidizing secondary alcohols, so III is wrong.
p1.flag: Alcohol dehydration to alkenes is not explicitly in the 2025 guide.

p1.key: From the reactions, oxidizing strength: Ag⁺ > Cu²⁺ > Fe²⁺ > Zn²⁺, and reducing strength: Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag. Strongest oxidizing agent Ag⁺(aq), strongest reducing agent Zn(s). Ag(s) is a metal atom, not an oxidizing agent.

Oxidation always occurs at the anode. In a voltaic cell the anode is the negative electrode; in an electrolytic cell the anode is the positive electrode. A and B swap the two cell types; D puts reduction at the positive electrode of an electrolytic cell.
Fe³⁺/Fe²⁺ has the more positive E°, so Fe³⁺ is reduced and Sn²⁺ is oxidized. E°cell = 0.77 − 0.15 = +0.62 V (do not multiply E° by stoichiometric coefficients).
Overall: 2H2O → 2H2 + O2. 4 e⁻ produce 2 H2 but only 1 O2, so V(O2) = 8.4 ÷ 2 = 4.2 cm³.
Charge passed = current × time; the moles of metal = charge ÷ (charge on ion × F). So current, time and the charge on the metal ion all affect the amount of metal deposited.
p1.flag: Faraday calculations are not in the 2025 guide.

p1.key: Y releases CO<sub>2</sub> with carbonate, so Y is a carboxylic acid. A primary alcohol (propan-1-ol) is oxidized by excess dichromate to propanoic acid. C (secondary) gives a ketone; D (tertiary) is not oxidized; A is already an acid.
In VO²⁺: V − 2 = +2 → V = +4. In VO<sub>3</sub>⁻: V − 6 = −1 → V = +5. The oxidation state increases, so vanadium is oxidized from +4 to +5.
In electrolysis, electrical energy drives a non-spontaneous redox reaction. Ions (not electrons) carry charge through the molten salt; cations gain electrons and anions lose them.
Ag → Ag⁺ + e⁻ (×3); NO3⁻ + 4H⁺ + 3e⁻ → NO + 2H2O. Overall: 3Ag + NO3⁻ + 4H⁺ → 3Ag⁺ + NO + 2H2O.
Tl⁺ is reduced (more positive E°) and V is oxidized. E°cell = E°(reduction) − E°(oxidation) = −0.34 − (−1.19) = +0.85 V. E° is not doubled for the 2Tl⁺.
Moles of metal = charge ÷ (z × F), and charge = current × time. A larger current or longer time increases the moles deposited; a higher ion charge z decreases the moles formed for the same charge.
p1.flag: Faraday calculations are not in the 2025 guide.

p1.key: Overall 2H2O → 2H2 + O2. n(H2) = 1 g ÷ 2 g mol⁻¹ = 0.5 mol, so n(O2) = 0.25 mol; mass = 0.25 × 32 = 8 g.

An oxidizing agent gains electrons. F<sub>2</sub> is the most electronegative element and most readily forms F⁻, so it is the strongest oxidizing agent. Halide ions (I⁻, F⁻) are reducing agents if anything.
Zn²⁺ is reduced and Mn oxidized. E°cell = E°(Zn²⁺/Zn) − E°(Mn²⁺/Mn) = −0.76 − (−1.18) = +0.42 V; positive, so the reaction is spontaneous.
Tertiary alcohols such as (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>COH have no H on the C–OH carbon, so they are not oxidized by acidified dichromate. A and C are primary, B is secondary.

In CaH<sub>2</sub> hydrogen gains an electron to form H⁻ (oxidation state 0 → −1), so H<sub>2</sub> is reduced and acts as the oxidizing agent. In B, C and D hydrogen is oxidized (0 → +1) and acts as a reducing agent.
In a voltaic cell a spontaneous redox reaction produces electrical energy. In an electrolytic cell electrical energy drives a non-spontaneous reaction. B, C and D swap these roles.
Cr2O7²⁻ + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr³⁺ + 7H2O; 6Cl⁻ → 3Cl2 + 6e⁻. Overall: Cr2O7²⁻ + 6Cl⁻ + 14H⁺ → 2Cr³⁺ + 3Cl2 + 7H2O.

Water is electrolysed: O<sub>2</sub> forms at the positive electrode (anode, 2H<sub>2</sub>O → O<sub>2</sub> + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻) and H<sub>2</sub> at the negative electrode (4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H<sub>2</sub>). Same charge gives 1 mol O<sub>2</sub> : 2 mol H<sub>2</sub>.

Reducing a carboxylic acid or an aldehyde (e.g. with LiAlH<sub>4</sub> or NaBH<sub>4</sub> for aldehydes) gives a primary alcohol. Ketones are reduced (not oxidized) to secondary alcohols; tertiary alcohols cannot be made this way; water adds to alkenes, not alkanes.
Oxidation states: MnCl2 +2, MnO2 +4, Mn2O3 +3, MnSO4 +2. Highest is MnO2.
In molten NaBr the ions are free to move randomly even with no current. When current flows, Br− moves to the positive electrode and loses electrons (oxidation), so A, B and C are all wrong. D.
Balanced: 3Cu + 2NO3− + 8H+ → 3Cu2+ + 2NO + 4H2O. Cu loses 2e− and N gains 3e− (+5 → +2), so 3Cu : 2NO, then balance O with water and H with H+.
The SHE uses H2 at 100 kPa (1 atm), 298 K and [H+] = 1.00 mol dm−3. 1.00 mol dm−3 H2SO4 would give about 2 mol dm−3 H+, so III is wrong. A.
In KNO2: +1 + N + 2(−2) = 0, so N = +3. NH4Cl: −3; HNO3: +5; N2O4: +4.
Q is connected to the positive terminal (anode). Cl− ions move there and lose electrons: 2Cl− → Cl2 + 2e−, which is oxidation. D.
Standard conditions for the SHE: 298 K, [H+] = 1 mol dm−3 and H2 gas at 100 kPa. Hydrogen is specified by its pressure, not by a concentration, so III is wrong. A.

Anode: Br2 forms in both (E° of Br2 is lower than O2, so Br− is oxidized in preference to water): same. Cathode: molten gives Mg, but in aqueous solution water is reduced to H2 because Mg2+ (−2.37 V) is very hard to reduce: different.

Hydration of propene gives mainly propan-2-ol, CH3CH(OH)CH3 (Markovnikov). Oxidizing this secondary alcohol gives the ketone propanone. Propan-1-ol (D) would oxidize to propanal/propanoic acid instead. C.
Fe goes from +2 (FeSO4) to +3 (Fe2(SO4)3), so FeSO4 is oxidized and is the reducing agent. O in H2O2 goes from −1 to −2, so H2O2 is the oxidizing agent. H2SO4 only provides H+.

E° is measured by connecting a half-cell (electrode in 1.0 mol dm−3 of its ions, standard conditions) to the standard hydrogen electrode, with a high-resistance voltmeter between them. All three are needed. D.

In electroplating, Ag+ ions are reduced and deposited on the object, so the spoon must be the negative electrode (cathode). The silver electrode is the positive electrode (anode), which dissolves to replace the Ag+.
Br goes from −1 in Br− to +5 in BrO3−, so Br− is oxidized and is the reducing agent. Mn is reduced (+7 → +4), so MnO4− is the oxidizing agent.
In a voltaic cell the positive electrode is where reduction (gain of electrons) occurs. Zn2+ → Zn and Cl2 → Cl− are reductions; Mg → Mg2+ is oxidation. A.
Fe3+ is reduced (cathode) and Cr is oxidized (anode). E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = 0.77 − (−0.74) = +1.51 V. Multiplying the Fe half-equation by 3 does not change E°.
Mn goes from +7 in MnO4− to +2 in Mn2+, so MnO4− is reduced (gains electrons) and is the oxidizing agent. Fe2+ loses electrons to it.
A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its salt: Fe > Ni, Zn > Fe and Ni > Pb. Increasing reactivity: Pb < Ni < Fe < Zn.
Mn has the more negative E°, so it is oxidized (anode) and Pb2+ is reduced. E°cell = −0.13 − (−1.19) = +1.06 V. 1.32 V would come from wrongly adding the two values.
Cathode: Cu2+ + 2e− → Cu. Anode (inert): 2H2O → O2 + 4H+ + 4e−. 4 mol e− make 2 Cu for every 1 O2, so Cu : O2 = 2 : 1. No H2 forms, as Cu2+ is reduced in preference to water.
For Zn to reduce Mg2+, E°cell = −2.37 − (−0.76) = −1.61 V, which is negative, so it is not spontaneous. Zn cannot oxidize Cl⁻ either, so no reaction occurs.

Reduction means a decrease in oxidation state. N in NO<sub>2</sub> is +4; in NO<sub>3</sub>⁻ it is +5, so NO<sub>3</sub>⁻ → NO<sub>2</sub> is a reduction. N<sub>2</sub>O (+1), HNO<sub>2</sub> (+3) and NO (+2) would need oxidation.
The SHE uses H<sub>2</sub> gas at 100 kPa (1 atm), [H⁺] = 1 mol dm⁻³ and 298 K, with a platinum (not carbon) electrode coated in platinum black.
In IO3⁻, I + 3(−2) = −1, so I = +5. In I2 it is 0. A decrease in oxidation number from +5 to 0 is reduction.
Y and Z both displace X, so X is least reactive. Z cannot displace Y, so Y is more reactive than Z. Order: X < Z < Y.
The more negative couple (Al) is oxidized: 2Al + 3Ni2+ → 2Al3+ + 3Ni. E°cell = −0.23 − (−1.66) = +1.43 V. 1.89 V comes from wrongly adding the potentials.
Mg<sup>2+</sup> + 2e⁻ → Mg and 2Cl⁻ → Cl<sub>2</sub> + 2e⁻ both use 2 mol e⁻ per mole, so the amounts of Mg and Cl<sub>2</sub> are equal. The same charge gives 2 mol Na (Na⁺ + e⁻ → Na) per mol Mg.
p1.flag: quantitative electrolysis not explicit in 2025 syllabus

p1.key: A more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one. Y displaces X (Y > X) and X displaces Z (X > Z). The second equation should read ZCl + Y → YCl + Z (Y > Z). Order: Y > X > Z.
p1.flag: misprint in question: second equation printed as YCl + Z → YCl + Z

p1.key: Charge Q = It. B: 2.0 × 250 = 500 C → 500/96 500 = 5.2 × 10⁻³ mol Ag × 108 = 0.56 g. C: 750 C → 3.9 × 10⁻³ mol Cu (2e⁻ each) × 63.5 = 0.25 g. Ag needs only 1 e⁻ per atom and is heavier, so B gives most.
p1.flag: quantitative electrolysis (Faraday) not explicit in 2025 syllabus

p1.key: The SHE needs [H⁺] = 1 mol dm⁻³. 1 mol dm⁻³ H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> would give about 2 mol dm⁻³ H⁺ (diprotic), so it is not a requirement. Platinum, 298 K and ~100 kPa H<sub>2</sub> are all required.

Reduction is gain of electrons, with electrons on the left. Cr in Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> goes from +6 to +3: Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> + 14H⁺ + 6e⁻ → 2Cr<sup>3+</sup> + 7H<sub>2</sub>O. B is the oxidation half-equation.

Cu<sup>2+</sup> is reduced at the copper electrode, which is therefore the positive electrode (cathode); a voltaic cell converts chemical to electrical energy. Electrons flow Zn → Cu externally, so anions in the salt bridge move towards the zinc half-cell; II is false.
A spontaneous reaction has E°cell > 0 (ΔG° < 0). Fe3+ oxidizes Br⁻, so Fe3+ is the better oxidizing agent than Br2 (and Br⁻ is the better reducing agent than Fe2+).
The object to be plated is the cathode, where Ag⁺ + e⁻ → Ag. The anode is silver, which dissolves to replace Ag⁺, and the electrolyte must contain Ag⁺ ions (silver nitrate).
Propanal can be oxidized to propanoic acid (I) and reduced to propan-1-ol (III). It is made by oxidizing propan-1-ol, not ethanol, so II is false (ethanol gives ethanal).

Sn<sup>2+</sup> is oxidized (+2 → +4 in SnO<sub>2</sub>) so it is the reducing agent. Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub><sup>2−</sup> is reduced (+6 → +3), so it is the oxidizing agent; it does not undergo oxidation.
Cu is oxidized (anode, negative) and Ag⁺ is reduced at the Ag cathode. Electrons flow externally from Cu to Ag, and Ag⁺ ions in solution move towards the Ag electrode where they are discharged.
Sn4+/Sn2+ has the more positive E°, so Sn4+ is reduced and Pb is oxidized: Sn4+ + Pb → Sn2+ + Pb2+. E°cell = +0.13 − (−0.13) = +0.26 V.
In series the same charge flows. Moles e⁻ = moles Ag = 1.00/107.87. Cu<sup>2+</sup> needs 2e⁻, so moles Cu = (1.00/107.87) ÷ 2, and mass Cu = (1.00/107.87) × 63.55/2 g.
p1.flag: Faraday's law calculations not explicit in 2025 syllabus

p1.key: Stage 1: OH⁻ substitutes Cl, giving butan-1-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>3</sub>OH. Stage 2: refluxing a primary alcohol with acidified dichromate oxidizes it fully to butanoic acid, CH<sub>3</sub>(CH<sub>2</sub>)<sub>2</sub>COOH (4 C). A gives a 5-carbon acid.
Mn is manganese (Mg is magnesium). In MnO<sub>2</sub> each O is −2, so Mn is +4: manganese(IV) oxide.

Zn loses electrons (it is oxidized) at the negative electrode. The electrons flow through the external circuit to the lead electrode, where Pb<sup>2+</sup> is reduced and Pb is deposited, so its mass increases. All three statements are correct.
E°cell = E°(reduction, MnO4−) − E°(oxidation, Fe3+/Fe2+) = 1.51 − 0.77 = +0.74 V. Multiplying the half-equation by 5 does not change E°.
A reaction is spontaneous if E°cell is positive. In C, Fe3+ (+0.77 V) is reduced and Fe (−0.45 V) is oxidized: E°cell = 0.77 − (−0.45) = +1.22 V. A, B and D all give negative values.

Primary alcohols are oxidized to aldehydes (with distillation) and then to carboxylic acids, so butan-1-ol gives butanal. Propan-1-ol cannot give a ketone. Secondary alcohols (pentan-2-ol, butan-2-ol) give ketones, not acids or aldehydes.
A reducing agent gives electrons to another species and so is itself oxidized (it loses electrons).
The mass deposited depends on the charge passed (current × time), the charge on the ion (electrons per atom) and the molar mass of the metal. The physical size of the ion has no effect.
p1.flag: quantitative electrolysis (Faraday) not in 2025 syllabus

p1.key: A voltaic cell turns the chemical energy of a spontaneous redox reaction into electrical energy, and oxidation happens at the anode (negative electrode). The salt bridge conducts by the movement of ions, not electrons, so III is false.
I2/I− (+0.54 V) is more positive than Sn4+/Sn2+ (+0.15 V), so I2 can oxidize Sn2+ to Sn4+: E°cell = +0.39 V. I2 cannot oxidize Fe2+ because Fe3+/Fe2+ is more positive (+0.77 V).

The oxidation state of I falls from +5 in IO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> to 0 in I<sub>2</sub>, so IO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> is reduced and is the oxidizing agent. SO<sub>2</sub> (S +4 → +6) is the reducing agent.
Ni loses electrons (Ni → Ni<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup>), so it is oxidized. Oxidation happens at the anode, which in a voltaic cell is the negative electrode.

In electroplating, the metal ions (Au<sup>+</sup>/Au<sup>3+</sup>) are reduced onto the object, so the object must be the cathode (negative electrode). The gold is the anode, which dissolves to replace the ions.
Mn is manganese (Mg is magnesium). In MnO<sub>2</sub> each O is −2, so Mn is +4: manganese(IV) oxide.

Cl goes from +1 in ClO<sup>−</sup> to 0 in Cl<sub>2</sub>, so ClO<sup>−</sup> is reduced and is the oxidizing agent. Cr goes from +3 to +6, so Cr(OH)<sub>3</sub> is oxidized and is the reducing agent.
Fe3+/Fe2+ has the more positive E°, so Fe3+ is reduced while Sn is oxidized. E°cell = 0.77 − (−0.14) = +0.91 V. Doubling the Fe half-equation does not double E°, so 1.68 V (D) is wrong.

At the cathode, water is reduced in preference to K<sup>+</sup>: 2H<sub>2</sub>O + 2e<sup>−</sup> → H<sub>2</sub> + 2OH<sup>−</sup>. Reduction occurs and H<sub>2</sub> is evolved. Cl<sub>2</sub> forms at the anode, leaving OH<sup>−</sup> behind, so the pH increases.

MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup> + 8H<sup>+</sup> + 5e<sup>−</sup> → Mn<sup>2+</sup> + 4H<sub>2</sub>O. Mn is reduced from +7 to +2, so electrons go on the reactant side. H<sup>+</sup> is added to the reactants to remove the O atoms as H<sub>2</sub>O, which appears in the products.

In KMnO<sub>4</sub>: +1 + Mn + 4(−2) = 0, so Mn = +7: potassium manganate(VII). In K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>: 2(+1) + 2Cr + 7(−2) = 0, so Cr = +6: potassium dichromate(VI). A uses non-systematic names with no oxidation numbers.

Electroplating (coating an object with a metal) uses electrolysis. Iron is extracted by reduction with carbon in a blast furnace, graphite is not made by electrolysis, and electric energy comes from voltaic cells, not electrolytic ones.
E°cell = E°(Ag+/Ag) − E°(Ni2+/Ni). So 1.06 = E°(Ag+/Ag) − (−0.26), giving E°(Ag+/Ag) = +0.80 V.
Cl goes from +5 in ClO3− to +4 in ClO2, so ClO3− is reduced and is the oxidizing agent. S goes from +4 in SO2 to +6 in HSO4−, so SO2 is oxidized (the reducing agent).
In molten PbBr2, Pb2+ ions gain electrons at the cathode to form Pb(l), and Br− ions lose electrons at the anode to form Br2(g). A and B list the ions, not the products.

A species reduces H<sup>+</sup> if it is a stronger reducing agent than H<sub>2</sub>, i.e. it is on the right of a half-equation with E° below 0.00 V. Sn(s) (E° = −0.14 V) qualifies: E°cell = +0.14 V. Fe<sup>2+</sup> has E° = +0.77 V, so it cannot.

The same charge passes in each case, i.e. the same number of moles of electrons. K+ + e− → K needs only 1 electron per atom, compared with 2 for Mg and Ca and 3 for Al, so the most moles of K are produced.

In NaH, hydrogen is −1 (hydride); it is oxidized to 0 in H<sub>2</sub>, while H in water (+1) is reduced to 0. B, C and D involve no change in oxidation states (decomposition, precipitation and acid–base).

Ions move through the salt bridge to keep each half-cell electrically neutral and complete the circuit. In a voltaic cell oxidation occurs at the negative anode, and the cell produces electricity spontaneously, so it needs no power supply and is not electrolytic.
For a spontaneous redox reaction E°cell is positive, and since ΔG° = −nFE°, ΔG° is negative.
E°cell = E°(reduction, Cl2) − E°(oxidation, Fe) = +1.36 − (−0.45) = +1.81 V. Electrode potentials are not multiplied by the stoichiometric coefficients.
Converting –C≡N to –CH2NH2 adds 2 H2, a reduction. It needs hydrogen with a metal catalyst such as Ni; H2 alone reacts too slowly, and H2O/H+ would hydrolyse the nitrile to a carboxylic acid.
p1.flag: Nitrile reduction not explicitly in 2025 guide

p1.key: Zn goes from 0 to +2 (oxidized) and H from +1 to 0 (reduced). A is ligand exchange (Cu stays +2), B is precipitation and D is an acid–base change with Cr staying +6.
IO3− (I +5) gains 5e− to form I (0); each I− loses 1e−, so 5 I− are needed per IO3−. IO3− + 5I− + 6H+ → 3I2 + 3H2O.
For 2Cu+ → Cu + Cu2+: reduction Cu+/Cu (+0.52 V), oxidation Cu+ → Cu2+ (+0.15 V). E°cell = 0.52 − 0.15 = +0.37 V, positive, so the disproportionation is spontaneous. D is the reverse (E° = −0.37 V).

In both solutions water is oxidized at the anode to O2 (4 e− per O2), so the same charge gives the same volume of O2. CuSO4 gives Cu, not H2, at the cathode; mol Cu = mol H2 (both 2e−), so C is wrong; CuSO4 solution becomes more acidic.
Cr goes from +6 in Cr2O72− to +3 in Cr2O3, so it is reduced. N goes from −3 to 0 (oxidized); H and O are unchanged.
Reduction is the gain of electrons, which lowers the oxidation number.
VO2+ is reduced to V3+ (E° = +0.34 V) and V2+ is oxidized to V3+ (reverse of the −0.26 V half-equation). E°cell = +0.34 − (−0.26) = +0.60 V.
SO42− is very hard to oxidize, so water is oxidized at the anode: 2H2O → O2 + 4H+ + 4e−, giving oxygen. Hydrogen forms at the cathode.
Mn is manganese (Mg is magnesium). In MnO2, x + 2(−2) = 0, so x = +4: manganese(IV) oxide.

In a voltaic cell the spontaneous reaction drives electrons from the negative anode to the positive cathode. In an electrolytic cell the power supply pushes electrons into the negative cathode, coming from the positive anode. A, B and C are true for both cells.

H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>(aq): H<sup>+</sup>/water is reduced to H<sub>2</sub> at the cathode, and since SO<sub>4</sub><sup>2−</sup> is not oxidized, water is oxidized to O<sub>2</sub> at the anode. Concentrated KI gives I<sub>2</sub>, concentrated NaCl gives Cl<sub>2</sub>, and AgNO<sub>3</sub> gives Ag.
Charge passed = (I/2) × 2t = It, the same as for copper. Cu2+ needs 2e− per atom but Ag+ needs only 1e−, so twice as many moles of Ag are deposited: 2z.
p1.flag: Faraday-type quantitative electrolysis not explicitly in 2025 guide

p1.key: (CH3)3CCHO is an aldehyde: NaBH4 reduces it to a primary alcohol, and acidified dichromate oxidizes it to a carboxylic acid. A secondary alcohol (A) can only be oxidized, a ketone (D) only reduced, and a tertiary alcohol (C) neither.
Mn goes from +7 in MnO4− to +2 in Mn2+: its oxidation state decreases, so MnO4− is reduced and is the oxidizing agent. N goes from +3 to +5, so NO2− is the reducing agent.

Zn is oxidized (anode), so electrons flow through the wire from Zn to Cu, and Cu2+ is used up. Ions, not electrons, move in the salt bridge: anions move towards the zinc half-cell to balance the Zn2+ being formed.
ΔG° = −nFE°cell, so a spontaneous reaction has E°cell positive and ΔG° negative.

In electroplating, the object to be plated (iron) is the negative electrode (cathode), and the plating metal, silver, is the positive electrode (anode). The electrolyte must contain Ag+, and oxidation occurs at the positive electrode.
Step 1: propanal is reduced to propan-1-ol by NaBH4 (K2Cr2O7 would oxidize it). Step 2: the alcohol reacts with methanoic acid to form an ester, a condensation (nucleophilic substitution).
Oxidation = increase in oxidation state. In N2O, N is +1; in NO it is +2, so N2O → NO is oxidation. The others are reductions: Cl +7→+5, N 0→−3, S +6→+4.
Pb goes from 0 to +2 (oxidized, II true) and Pb in PbO2 goes from +4 to +2, so PbO2 is the oxidizing agent (III true). H stays +1 throughout, so H+ is not reduced (I false).

Ag+ is reduced and Ni is oxidized, so Ag has the more positive E°. Electrons flow from Ni to Ag; oxidation of Ni happens at the negative electrode, which is the anode (not cathode), and reduction of Ag+ is at the positive cathode.
Water is electrolysed: cathode 4H2O + 4e− → 2H2 + 4OH−; anode 2H2O → O2 + 4H+ + 4e−. For the same charge, n(O2) = ½ n(H2), so 0.1 mol H2 gives 0.05 mol O2 at the anode.
Reducing an aldehyde (e.g. with NaBH4) gives a primary alcohol with the same carbon skeleton: CH3CH2CH(CH3)CHO → 2-methylbutan-1-ol. D is the oxidation product.
Cu is below hydrogen in the activity series, so it cannot displace H2 from acid. Zn (above H) gives H2; Na2CO3 (a carbonate) and CuO (a basic oxide) both react with HCl.
Cr goes from +6 in Cr2O72− to +3 in Cr2O3, so chromium is reduced. N is oxidized (−3 → 0); H (+1) and O (−2) do not change.
D is an acid–base neutralization: no oxidation states change. A (C −4 → −2), B (C 0 → +4) and C (disproportionation of C +2 to +4 and 0) all involve electron transfer.
Measured against Zn, every potential shifts by +0.76 V: E = +0.34 − (−0.76) = +1.10 V. This equals the E°cell of a Zn–Cu cell.
E is the anode in CuSO4(aq): O2 forms (4e− per O2). F is the cathode in H2SO4(aq): H2 forms (2e− per H2). In series the same charge passes, so O2 : H2 = 1 : 2.
All three can be reduced: ethene to ethane (hydrogenation), ethanoic acid to ethanol (LiAlH4) and ethanal to ethanol (NaBH4 or LiAlH4).
In A, Mg is oxidized (0 → +2) and Al3+ is reduced (+3 → 0). B is acid–base, C is precipitation and D is thermal decomposition; no oxidation states change in these.
MnO4−/Mn2+ has the more positive E° (+1.51 V), so MnO4− is reduced and I− reduces MnO4− to Mn2+, being oxidized to I2. The colour goes from purple to brown.
Cathode: Cu2+ is more easily reduced than water, so Cu(s) is deposited. Anode: sulfate is not oxidized; water is, giving O2(g) (2H2O → O2 + 4H+ + 4e−).
In Cr2O72−: 2Cr + 7(−2) = −2, so Cr = +6. In Cr2O3: 2Cr + 3(−2) = 0, so Cr = +3.
NaBH4 reduces a ketone to a secondary alcohol with the OH on the same carbon: pentan-2-one → pentan-2-ol.
Butan-2-ol, CH3CH2CH(OH)CH3, is a secondary alcohol, oxidized to butanone. The ketone (A), tertiary alcohol (C) and carboxylic acid (D) are not oxidized by acidified dichromate.
In H2O2, O is −1; in H2O it is −2, so oxygen is reduced (and I− is oxidized to I2). In A, O is oxidized (0 → +2 in F2O); B and D involve no change for O.
Ca2+ is far harder to reduce than water, so H2 forms at the cathode. In concentrated bromide solution, Br− is oxidized at the anode to bromine in preference to O2.
The object must be the cathode, connected to the negative terminal (Y), and the copper anode connected to the positive terminal (X). The electrolyte must contain Cu2+: CuSO4(aq).

Mass of product depends on the charge passed (current × time) and the charge on the ions (moles of electrons per mole of product). The initial mass of the cathode has no effect on how much is deposited.
p1.flag: Faraday-type quantitative electrolysis not in 2025 guide

p1.key: Cu is below H in the activity series, so it cannot displace hydrogen from dilute H2SO4. CuO (a basic oxide) and CuCO3 (a carbonate) react with acids as bases, forming CuSO4 + water (+ CO2 for the carbonate).
Oxidation is loss of electrons, gain of oxygen, loss of hydrogen or an increase in oxidation number. Options B, C and D all describe reduction.
Molten ZnBr2 contains only Zn2+ and Br−. Zn2+ is reduced at the cathode to zinc, and Br− is oxidized at the anode to bromine. There is no water, so hydrogen cannot form.
Cell 1: Ag+ + e− → Ag, so n(e−) = x/108. The same charge passes through cell 2, where 2H2O → O2 + 4H+ + 4e−, so n(O2) = ¼ × x/108. Volume = x/108 × ¼ × 22.7 dm3.
p1.flag: quantitative electrolysis (amounts of product vs charge) is not explicitly in the 2025 syllabus

p1.key: At the cathode water is reduced in preference to K+ (K is very reactive), giving hydrogen. At the anode the concentrated I− is oxidized more easily than water, giving iodine.
P goes from 0 in P4 to −3 in PH3 (reduced) and to +1 in H2PO2− (oxidized). This is disproportionation: P4 is both the oxidizing and the reducing agent. The oxidation states of H and O do not change.
Oxidation at the anode releases electrons, which travel through the external wire from the anode (−) to the cathode (+). The salt bridge carries ions, not electrons.
If E° is negative, ΔG° = −nFE° is positive. Then from ΔG° = −RT ln K, ln K is negative, so K < 1 and the reaction is not spontaneous as written.
Hg2+ is reduced (cathode) and Cr is oxidized (anode). E°cell = E°(cathode) − E°(anode) = +0.85 − (−0.74) = +1.59 V. Multiplying the half-equations by 3 or 2 does not change E°.

Acidified MnO4− oxidizes primary and secondary alcohols. I (butan-1-ol) and II ((CH3)3CCH2OH, OH on a CH2) are primary and III (butan-2-ol) is secondary, so all three decolourize it. Only tertiary alcohols would not react.
At the anode Cl− is oxidized: 2Cl− → Cl2(g) + 2e−. Chlorine exists as diatomic molecules, not as single Cl atoms, and sodium forms at the cathode.
Oxidation always takes place at the anode. In a voltaic cell the anode releases electrons into the circuit, so it is the negative electrode.

The amount of product depends on the total charge passed (Q = I × t), so current and time both matter. The charge on the cation sets how many electrons are needed per atom deposited, e.g. 1 for Na+ and 2 for Cu2+.
p1.flag: quantitative electrolysis (Faraday) is not in the 2025 syllabus

p1.key: The SHE needs H2 at 100 kPa, [H+] = 1 mol dm−3, 298 K and a platinum electrode. The volume of solution does not affect the potential, so it is not a requirement.
Only primary alcohols can be oxidized to carboxylic acids. Butan-1-ol is primary. Propan-2-ol and pentan-3-ol are secondary (giving ketones), and 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary (not oxidized).
In H2SO4: 2(+1) + S + 4(−2) = 0, so S = +6. SO2 and H2SO3 have S = +4, and H2S has S = −2.
Mg is oxidized (loses electrons) at the anode: Mg → Mg2+ + 2e−. Ag+ is reduced at the cathode: Ag+ + e− → Ag. This matches the overall equation.

The strongest oxidizing agent is the species on the left of the half-equation with the most positive (least negative) E°. −0.13 V > −1.66 V, so Pb2+ is the stronger oxidizing agent. Pb and Al are reducing agents.
At the cathode, water is reduced rather than K+ (K is very reactive), giving H2. At the anode, the concentrated Br− is oxidized in preference to water, giving Br2.
Reduction (e.g. with NaBH4) adds hydrogen to the C=O. The carbonyl carbon of a ketone is bonded to two carbon groups, so the product is a secondary alcohol. Aldehydes give primary alcohols.
In SO32−, S + 3(−2) = −2, so S = +4. In SOCl2, S + (−2) + 2(−1) = 0, so S = +4. In S2O32− S is +2, in SO42− it is +6, and in H2S it is −2.
X displaces Y, so X is more reactive than Y. X cannot displace Z, so Z is more reactive than X. Increasing reactivity: Y < X < Z.
At the positive electrode (anode), the concentrated Br− is oxidized in preference to water, giving Br2. At the negative electrode, water is reduced rather than the very reactive Na+, giving H2.
The same charge passes through each cell in series. For 2 mol e−: Ag+ + e− gives 2 Ag; Cu2+ + 2e− gives 1 Cu; 2H+ + 2e− gives 1 H2. Ratio 2 : 1 : 1.
p1.flag: quantitative electrolysis (moles vs charge) not explicitly in the 2025 syllabus

p1.key: Reducing a carboxylic acid goes via an aldehyde: butanoic acid → butanal (→ butan-1-ol). Butanone reduces to a secondary alcohol, and the alcohols are already fully reduced (they would be oxidized, not reduced, to carbonyls).
In H2O2: 2(+1) + 2x = 0, so x = −1. The O–O bond means oxygen is not −2 here (a peroxide).
In molten KCl, Cl− is oxidized at the anode to Cl2 (2Cl− → Cl2 + 2e−) and K+ is reduced at the cathode to K. Chlorine is released as diatomic molecules, not atoms.
Measure relative to the new reference: E = E°(Mn2+/Mn) − E°(Fe3+/Fe2+) = −1.18 − (+0.77) = −1.95 V.
With copper electrodes, the copper anode is oxidized (Cu → Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup>) and loses mass, while Cu<sup>2+</sup> is reduced and deposited on the cathode, which gains mass.

Reducing a ketone gives a secondary alcohol: CH<sub>3</sub>COC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> → CH<sub>3</sub>CH(OH)C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>. An aldehyde (C) gives a primary alcohol and a carboxylic acid (A) gives a primary alcohol.
Carbon gains hydrogen and loses chlorine (its oxidation state falls from −2 to −4), so CH<sub>3</sub>Cl is reduced; the Cl atom is replaced by H, which is substitution.
Electrons flow round the external circuit into terminal X, so X is the positive terminal; in the cell, reduction happens there, so it is the cathode.
Mn + Zn2+ = (Mn + 2Ag+) − (Cu + 2Ag+) − (Zn + Cu2+), so E° = 1.98 − 0.46 − 1.10 = 0.42 V.
Cells in series pass the same charge. Per mole of electrons: Ag<sup>+</sup> gives 108 g, Cu<sup>2+</sup> gives 64/2 = 32 g, Sb<sup>3+</sup> gives 122/3 ≈ 40.7 g. Order: Cu < Sb < Ag.
p1.flag: quantitative electrolysis (charge/mass) not in 2025 guide

p1.key: LiAlH4 is a reducing agent; reducing an aldehyde gives a primary alcohol, propan-1-ol.

Bi goes from +5 in BiO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> to +3 in Bi<sup>3+</sup>, so BiO<sub>3</sub><sup>−</sup> is reduced and is the oxidizing agent. Mn<sup>2+</sup> (+2 → +7 in MnO<sub>4</sub><sup>−</sup>) is the reducing agent.
A voltaic cell converts chemical energy into electrical energy using a spontaneous redox reaction. Non-spontaneous redox reactions are driven in electrolytic cells.
The SHE is the reference electrode and is assigned E° = 0 V by definition, whether written as reduction or oxidation.

A copper anode dissolves (Cu → Cu<sup>2+</sup> + 2e<sup>−</sup>), replacing the Cu<sup>2+</sup> deposited at the cathode, so copper keeps depositing until the anode is used up. With an inert anode only the Cu<sup>2+</sup> already in solution can be deposited.
